note: Objectively answerable: lower-back support throughout the film is more precise than general comfort. Let learners select supporting words rather than meeting a three-word gate. Feedback should distinguish support from softness as well as size.

Poorly defined: advice for mystery fans is not a promise about their reaction. Split into matching the likely audience and distinguishing a recommendation from a guarantee. The friendly-register feedback is useful once both decisions are explicit.

The question asks for a place that neither version narrows. The texts also differ in certainty and strength. Ask which part limits the claim to around lunchtime and compare “gets” with “can get” separately. Check each independently.

Open production is useful if focused: substitute one phrase describing the mood and say what it changes. “Busy atmosphere” shifts meaning, while “pleasant atmosphere” weakens specificity. The note explains mood but supplies no usable comparison. Use example-led self-review.

Here fair pricing is distinct from cheapness; the text gives no actual price. Compare two in-context alternatives with different strength and explain the author’s inference. The length gate accepts irrelevant writing.
The food offset the delay; it did not shorten it. The gloss “compensated for” is harder than the phrase. Check the two interpretations before asking for optional paraphrase.

“Go when it is less busy” retains advice without inventing a time. A simple meaning check is sufficient, with self-reviewed paraphrase optional. The feedback gives a gloss but misses the practical recommendation.
Make optional or combine with price and access vocabulary. “Nearby” loses the walking mode. A contrast with “a short drive” tests what readers can infer; the note otherwise repeats the phrase.

Keep texture practice, but offer in-sentence comparisons of crunchy, fresh and juicy. The feedback rightly distinguishes texture from taste. Avoid asking learners to replace a precise term merely to meet a length target.

Ask which revision still identifies the wait as the biggest problem. “A disadvantage” loses priority. Replace the harder gloss “principal disadvantage” with an example and combine with another strength-of-criticism task if needed.

An alternative must preserve portion and price, not just “good lunch”. Let students check both meanings separately, then self-review a short rewrite. The note names the distinction but gives no example.

“Opening scene” is already the natural specific phrase. Requiring a replacement yields little review-writing practice. Make it an optional collocation note, and use the saved space for pacing vocabulary.

The special effects are praised for impressiveness, not their role in making dialogue realistic. Compare “impressive” and “expensive” in context. Feedback calling the phrase precise does not teach that distinction.

Good open task with a narrower instruction: keep this a mild criticism, then write a stronger version. Compare “a little slow” and “painfully slow”. The feedback identifies “rather” but needs a contrast learners can check.
“Fast-moving” need not mean action throughout. Ask which substitution preserves continuity. Keep optional after the pacing contrast to avoid another generic rewrite with the same goal.

“Worth a read” keeps the invitation without guaranteeing enjoyment. Have learners compare advice aimed at mystery fans and an overclaim for everyone. Current feedback neither models a replacement nor explains tone.

Retain an open transformation of the entire “so … that” sentence. “Clearly” can be accurate but loses mental imagery. Present a model explaining how the description lets the reader picture the setting.
Check idiomatic meaning first. The reader wants to continue, rather than physically struggling with a book. The gloss “gripping” can be equally unfamiliar. Follow with an optional paraphrase.

The location and performers are simple description. Replace compulsory paraphrasing with an optional glossary example distinguishing “featuring” from “organised by”. Neither the length gate nor another general rewrite improves evaluation here.

Lively fits; loud or fast alone changes the claim. Use a quick choice with feedback on what the energy describes. Consider combining with “outstanding performance” into one choice about different kinds of praise.

Distinguish stronger “outstanding” from positive but milder “enjoyable”, using the dancing as evidence. The note names a collocation without illustrating strength. A short sorted scale would make useful practice.

“Worth what it costs” preserves evaluation; “cheap” does not. Compare in context or consolidate with Riverside pricing. The paragraph claims value but supplies no actual ticket price, so avoid asking students to justify the amount.

The focus shown in the prompt omits “of experience”. Present the full phrase and compare “for beginners” with “for people with different experience levels”. The note’s “fitness” adds avoidable difficulty.

“Ready to try” can preserve the threshold; “fearless” exaggerates. Compare two natural alternatives and link the threshold to the demonstrations. The gloss is directionally right but does not show degree.

Few choices and few cheap choices are distinct. Let learners rewrite the full menu clause while preserving both. The feedback currently explains only variety. Review against one comparison example rather than counting words.

Teach the idiom in context with “get more out of your visit”. Contrast getting more enjoyment with staying longer. A short checked meaning task can replace the lengthy paraphrase and generic feedback.
“Get harder as you go” retains progression; “are very hard” does not. Feedback should say increasing difficulty need not be gradual. Compare the two phrasings, then self-review an optional rewrite.

The satisfaction follows solving a puzzle with effort. Compare “satisfying” with “relaxing” or “easy”. The feedback explains effort but skips how “genuinely” reinforces the judgement. Use an in-context degree comparison.

Contrast instructions that are confusing with instructions more confusing than they need to be. Preserve the restriction to some advanced challenges in any rewrite. Feedback identifies avoidability but does not check the scope.

Short levels support playing from time to time. “Best for beginners” changes audience and “perfect for everyone” generalises. Ask which rewrite preserves the playing pattern, with an optional brief self-review.

Use a strength scale for “more”, “much more” and “a little more” memorable; retain comparison with textbooks. Feedback correctly identifies the intensifier, but one focused comparison is better than repeating the same broad stem.

The writer sets a threshold for a named audience and also says the explanations do not sound childish. Preserve these across the full clause. Keep genuinely open rewriting and compare with a model using “easy for newcomers to follow”.

“Difficult ideas” loses the contrast with hands-on examples. Ask students to explain “abstract” in this museum context, with an optional one-phrase rewrite. The note names a collocation but does not explain meaning.
The sample meets the floor and two-sentence brief and retains back support, audibility and both prices. The natural measured criticism models the checklist. Keep independent revision and self-review.

The example meets 45–65 words, incorporates the handle and short labels and limits crowding by place and time. The advice assumes a quieter time exists. Qualify it and either request advice in the brief or remove that checklist demand. Distinguish the 30-word gate from the target.
The sample meets the floor and two-sentence brief, but “at the door” adds a location to “on arrival”. Replace that phrase, and retain the welcome and food checks as self-review.

The model meets the minimum and carries forward the three bands, twenty minutes, water and midday. Its lively-atmosphere judgement follows the observation without overstating it. All checklist points are visible in the two sentences.

The friendly conditional recommendation targets students who like solving changing rules. The model meets the minimum and explains why the fact matters. Keep as a distinct register task and record self-review.

The model fulfils the scope and targeted recommendation, and fits the range, but merges the diagnostic note and the extract. Label them separately, specify whether the note counts toward 35–55 words, and add a checklist check for keeping the exact number, setting and lighting.
